Noninferiority and Equivalence Decisions for a Budget Constrained Contrast

Source: R/seq_budget.R
decide_seq_budget.Rd

Four tests of the contrast estimated by seq_budget, for use once sampling has ended. Each is a one-sided test at level alpha_level (equivalence is two one-sided tests, each at that level), computed from the contrast estimate and its standard error. The noninferiority and equivalence functions are the tests of Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, and Padalunkal (2025). The superiority and inferiority functions are the one-sided tests against a single margin: the article's superiority test and its noninferiority test are special cases of the first, and the two together are the two halves of its equivalence test.

Usage

decide_seq_budget_noninferiority(check, margin, alpha_level = 0.05)

decide_seq_budget_superiority(check, margin, alpha_level = 0.05)

decide_seq_budget_inferiority(check, margin, alpha_level = 0.05)

decide_seq_budget_equivalence(
  check,
  margin_lower,
  margin_upper,
  alpha_level = 0.05
)

Arguments

check

An object returned by seq_budget. A check from any other procedure is refused.

margin

A single finite number on the scale of the contrast. For noninferiority it is the size of the noninferiority margin and must be positive; inferiority, the null hypothesis, is that the contrast is at or below -margin. For superiority and inferiority it is the value the contrast is compared with, given with its sign (negative, zero, or positive).

alpha_level

The one-sided level of the test: a single number strictly between 0 and 0.5 (default 0.05). For equivalence it is the level of each of the two one-sided tests.

margin_lower, margin_upper

For equivalence: the lower and upper equivalence margins, single finite numbers on the scale of the contrast given with their signs, with margin_lower < margin_upper (for example -3 and 3).

Value

A length one logical: TRUE if the null hypothesis is rejected, so that the alternative (noninferiority, superiority, inferiority, or equivalence) is supported, and FALSE otherwise. FALSE is not evidence for the null hypothesis.

Details

Write \(\psi\) for the population contrast, \(\hat{\psi}\) for its estimate (the contrast row of the check), \(\hat{V}\) for the estimated variance of the estimate (the variance row), and \(z_{\alpha}\) for the upper \(100\alpha\) percent point of the standard normal distribution, with \(\alpha\) the one-sided level alpha_level.

The level. Every decision is computed from those two rows of the check and alpha_level. None is read from the confidence limits printed on the check, which are two-sided at the check's conf_level, so a decision does not depend on that confidence level. The limits a decision compares with its margin, \(\hat{\psi} \pm z_{\alpha} \sqrt{\hat{V}}\), are those of a \(1 - 2\alpha\) interval: a 90 percent interval for the default alpha_level = 0.05, the level of the article's tables. This is how the sibling functions ss_seq_c and equivalence_c in DMAR state the level.

The direction. The article assumes that a larger response is better (p. 428), so code the contrast so that larger values of \(\psi\) favor the treatment of interest. If a smaller response is better, reverse the sign of every contrast weight first.

How close the level is to nominal. All four tests are asymptotic (the article relies on the central limit theorem, Appendix A), and their level is not exact in samples of realistic size. In simulations of the noninferiority test at nominal level 0.05 (10,000 studies per condition, standard error about 0.002; pilot of 10 per group; the true contrast exactly at the margin), the rejection rate was 0.050 to 0.057 for normal populations when the budget bought about 30 to 120 observations per group. In a smaller design with 15 to 28 per group it was about 0.058 (0.052 to 0.061 over seven such runs). A one-sided test is more sensitive to skewness than a two-sided interval: for skewed populations the rate ranged from 0.040 to 0.085, the largest where the groups with negative weights were small (about 29 and 48 observations). The inferiority test rejects in the other tail. In two of these designs (the normal row of the article's Table 1 with a budget of 5,000, and the smaller design) its rate at the margin was 0.054 and 0.059 for normal populations and 0.066 and 0.076 for right skewed ones; the noninferiority test in the same runs had 0.056 and 0.059, and 0.043 and 0.055. The equivalence test, with the true contrast on one of its margins, rejects at the rate of the corresponding one-sided test when the other margin is far away, and less often when the two margins are close. A smaller pilot raises the rates further; seq_budget_pilot has the figures for the noninferiority test. For normal populations the simulated power agreed with the article's Equation C9 (0.80 to 0.81 in five designs against 0.804). seq_budget_sensitivity reports the rejection rate for a design of interest.

When the decision is made. The level of each test is stated for one decision, made when sampling has ended. If the check says that sampling has not ended (is_satisfied is FALSE), the decision is still returned, with a warning that it is provisional. If the variance of a group is unusable (the check's variance_unusable attribute is TRUE: the observations in some group are all equal), the functions stop, whether or not the budget has ended the sampling, because the decision would rest on a variance of zero for that group.

Noninferiority

decide_seq_budget_noninferiority() is the article's test for noninferiority (Equations 6 and 7; in Appendix C, Equations C1 and C3). With \(\delta\) the margin, it tests \(H_0: \psi \le -\delta\) against \(H_A: \psi > -\delta\). In words, the null hypothesis is inferiority: the treatment of interest falls short of the comparison by the margin or more. The alternative is noninferiority: any shortfall is smaller than the margin. margin is the size of the margin, a positive number (the article's \(|\psi_0|\), "the least relevant value of the contrast"); the hypotheses are about -margin. The null hypothesis is rejected, and noninferiority is declared, when (Equation C3) $$\hat{\psi} > -\delta + z_{\alpha} \sqrt{\hat{V}}.$$ Noninferiority is the special case margin = -abs(delta) of the superiority test below: with delta the noninferiority margin, these two calls return the same decision at any alpha_level.

decide_seq_budget_noninferiority(check, margin = delta)
decide_seq_budget_superiority(check, margin = -abs(delta))

Superiority

decide_seq_budget_superiority() is the one-sided test that the contrast is above a margin \(m\): \(H_0: \psi \le m\) against \(H_A: \psi > m\). In words, the null hypothesis is that the contrast does not exceed the margin, and the alternative is that it does. margin is the value \(m\) itself, with its sign: it may be positive, zero, or negative. The null hypothesis is rejected when $$\hat{\psi} > m + z_{\alpha} \sqrt{\hat{V}}.$$ With a positive margin, \(m = |\psi_0|\), this is the article's test for superiority (Equations 8 and 9; Equations C2 and C4): the treatment of interest is better than the comparison by more than the margin. With margin = 0 it is the ordinary one-sided test that the contrast is positive. With a negative margin it is the noninferiority test above. With \(m\) the lower equivalence margin \(\psi_1\), it is the first of the two one-sided tests that make up the article's test for equivalence (Equations C11 and C13).

Inferiority

decide_seq_budget_inferiority() is the one-sided test that the contrast is below a margin \(m\): \(H_0: \psi \ge m\) against \(H_A: \psi < m\). In words, the null hypothesis is that the contrast is at or above the margin, and the alternative, the conclusion the data must establish, is that it is below the margin. margin is the value \(m\) itself, with its sign. The null hypothesis is rejected when $$\hat{\psi} < m - z_{\alpha} \sqrt{\hat{V}}.$$ This is the mirror image of the superiority test: reversing the sign of every contrast weight and of the margin turns one into the other. In the article these hypotheses and this rejection rule appear, with \(m\) the upper equivalence margin \(\psi_2\), as the second of the two one-sided tests that make up the test for equivalence (Equations C12 and C14). As a test on its own the article states the hypotheses once, in its footnote 1, with \(m = -|\psi_0|\), as the form its superiority test takes when a smaller response is better. When a larger response is better, margin = -delta declares the treatment of interest inferior by more than delta. This is not the article's noninferiority test, in which inferiority is the null hypothesis.

Equivalence

decide_seq_budget_equivalence() is the article's test for equivalence (Equation 11; in Appendix C, Equations C10 to C15). With \(\psi_1\) the lower and \(\psi_2\) the upper equivalence margin, it tests \(H_0: \psi \le \psi_1\) or \(\psi \ge \psi_2\) against \(H_A: \psi_1 < \psi < \psi_2\). In words, the null hypothesis is nonequivalence (the contrast is at or beyond one of the margins) and the alternative is equivalence (the contrast lies between them). margin_lower and margin_upper are the margins \(\psi_1\) and \(\psi_2\) themselves, with their signs: for equivalence within 3 points either way they are -3 and 3. The article takes \(\psi_1 < 0 < \psi_2\); only margin_lower < margin_upper is required here. The null hypothesis is rejected when (Equation C15) $$\psi_1 + z_{\alpha} \sqrt{\hat{V}} < \hat{\psi} < \psi_2 - z_{\alpha} \sqrt{\hat{V}}.$$ These are two one-sided tests, each at level \(\alpha\) (Equations C11 to C14): equivalence is declared exactly when the superiority test at margin_lower and the inferiority test at margin_upper, each at the same alpha_level, both reject.

References

Chattopadhyay, B., Bandyopadhyay, T., Kelley, K., & Padalunkal, J. J. (2025). A sequential approach for noninferiority or equivalence of a linear contrast under cost constraints. Psychological Methods, 30(2), 425–439. doi:10.1037/met0000570

Luh, W. M., & Guo, J. H. (2016). Sample size planning for the noninferiority or equivalence of a linear contrast with cost considerations. Psychological Methods, 21(1), 13–34. doi:10.1037/met0000039

See also

seq_budget. In DMAR, equivalence_c gives the fixed sample size equivalence and noninferiority tests for a contrast with the same one-sided alpha_level, and ss_seq_c plans a sequential fixed-width interval for those decisions.

Other seq_budget: seq_budget(), seq_budget_next(), seq_budget_optimal(), seq_budget_pilot(), seq_budget_sensitivity()

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu, Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in

Examples

# Is a cheaper online training format (group 1) no worse, by more than
# 3 points, than the average of two established formats?
set.seed(113)
weights <- c(1, -0.5, -0.5)
costs <- c(10, 38, 15)
true_means <- c(50, 50, 50)
scores <- lapply(true_means, function(m) rnorm(10, mean = m, sd = 6))
repeat {
  out <- seq_budget(scores, weights, cost_per_group = costs, budget = 3000)
  g <- seq_budget_next(out)
  if (is.na(g)) break
  scores[[g]] <- c(scores[[g]], rnorm(1, mean = true_means[g], sd = 6))
}
out
#> Sequential check (budget constrained K-population contrast)
#> 
#>   Current n       : 192
#>   Criterion n     : 194
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : -0.8960654
#>   contrast          : 0.8640861
#>   upper_limit       : 2.624238
#>   variance          : 0.8064992
#>   current_total_n   : 192
#>   current_total_cost: 2995
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE (sampling has ended: the budget is exhausted)
#> 
#>   Note: Sampling has ended because the budget cannot pay for another
#>         observation: 5 of 3000 is left, and one more observation from a
#>         group still below its criterion (groups 1 and 3) costs at least
#>         10.

# Noninferiority with a margin of 3 points, at one-sided level 0.05.
decide_seq_budget_noninferiority(out, margin = 3)
#> [1] TRUE

# The same test, as the special case margin = -abs(3) of superiority.
decide_seq_budget_superiority(out, margin = -abs(3))
#> [1] TRUE

# Is the online format better than the average of the other two at all,
# or worse than it?
decide_seq_budget_superiority(out, margin = 0)
#> [1] FALSE
decide_seq_budget_inferiority(out, margin = 0)
#> [1] FALSE

# Equivalence within 3 points either way: two one-sided tests at 0.05,
# and then at a much stricter level.
decide_seq_budget_equivalence(out, margin_lower = -3, margin_upper = 3)
#> [1] TRUE
decide_seq_budget_equivalence(out, margin_lower = -3, margin_upper = 3,
                              alpha_level = 0.005)
#> [1] FALSE
